description: Firekmok is a flood and waterlogging monitoring platform that uses a risk score to assess the severity of the situation. It provides an action plan for public officials and business owners.
summary:
Fire Mok is an intelligent flood monitoring platform designed to help communities and public authorities prepare for and respond to floods. Inspired by the devastating May 2024 floods in the Guaíba River Basin, in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, the project transforms satellite data into clear and useful information for disaster response.

Using radar images from NASA and ESA satellites, Fire Mok can detect flooded areas even when heavy clouds make it difficult for traditional satellites to capture images. The platform combines this information with weather forecasts, terrain data, and population information to identify areas at greater risk and understand which communities may need help first.

Fire Mok turns complex environmental data into easy-to-understand flood maps, before-and-after comparisons, and risk assessments for each municipality. It also provides practical recommendations to help public authorities prioritize emergency actions and protect the most vulnerable populations.

Our goal is to make satellite technology more accessible and useful, helping communities make faster, better-informed decisions and reduce the impact of future floods.
details:
Project Details

What does it do and how does it work?

Fire Mok is an intelligent flood monitoring and triage platform designed for environmental disaster management, anchored on the May 2024 Guaíba basin flood in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil.

The platform automatically ingests day-and-night, all-weather Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery—which is NISAR-ready—to detect surface water extent through dense cloud cover.

The data pipeline processes SAR radar backscatter (σ), applies context masks to eliminate false positives, and integrates topographic terrain susceptibility using Copernicus DEM and the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) model. It combines these physical layers with weather observations and forecasts from Open-Meteo and NASA POWER, alongside demographic vulnerability metrics from the IBGE 2022 Census and WorldPop exposure data.

The system outputs a municipal risk index (choropleth map) and generates data-traceable emergency action plans. Users interact with the platform through a React web application featuring interactive map layers, backscatter threshold adjustments, a before-and-after flood swipe tool, and municipal triage summary panels.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

The main benefit of Fire Mok is providing public managers and emergency responders with rapid, objective situational awareness during extreme rainfall events.

Because extreme storms bring heavy cloud cover that blinds conventional optical satellites, Fire Mok’s active microwave sensing ensures uninterrupted monitoring day and night.

Its intended impact is to empower local authorities to identify vulnerable communities early, prioritize rescue and relief logistics, and make data-driven policy decisions to protect human lives and critical infrastructure.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3.13 (69.4%), TypeScript (27.1%), and CSS.
  • Backend & Data Engineering: Python with uv package manager, FastAPI, rio-tiler for dynamic COG raster tile rendering, STAC API via Planetary Computer, ASF DAAC for NISAR HDF5 conversion, and Docker for containerization.
  • Frontend Development: React, Vite, MapLibre GL for web mapping, and static deployment via GitHub Pages.
  • Testing & Automation: GitHub Actions (daily scheduled data ingestion pipeline), pytest (87 pipeline tests, 9 API tests), and Vitest (20 frontend tests).
  • Datasets & External APIs: Sentinel-1 SAR (RTC), Copernicus DEM (HAND model), Open-Meteo API, NASA POWER, IBGE 2022 Census, WorldPop, ESA WorldCover 10m, and Sentinel-2 NDWI (for chip validation).

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider?

  • Creativity: Fire Mok bridges advanced radar remote sensing physics with granular socio-demographic census data, turning complex satellite backscatter into automated, human-readable municipal triage scores and data-backed action plans.
  • Factors Considered:
    1. Optical Blindness: Traditional optical imagery fails during heavy rain; radar SAR was selected because its active microwave signals penetrate clouds day and night.
    2. Noise & False Positive Reduction: Radar signals suffer from urban corner-reflection and permanent water ambiguity; our team implemented ESA WorldCover 10m masks to clean the flood extents.
    3. Statistical Validation: SAR water extents were rigorously validated against Sentinel-2 NDWI chips using confusion matrices, F1 scores, IoU, and Cohen’s kappa with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
    4. Accessibility: To guarantee resilience, the system was designed with both a lightweight static web demo (mirrored pre-rendered tiles and JSON endpoints) and a full microservice API.
